content.title: About
content.content: Fish curry with rice is a fragrant Indian dish where tender pieces of fish are simmered in a spiced curry sauce and served over fluffy rice. The dish combines bold spices, coconut milk, and fresh herbs for a rich flavor and inviting aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Curry refers to a wide range of spice blends that can vary greatly in composition.
Traditional Indian fish curries often use freshwater or sea fish such as tilapia, snapper, or salmon.
Coconut milk, frequently added to the sauce, mellows the heat of the spices and gives the dish a creamy texture.
The dish is commonly served with basmati or jasmine rice, which absorbs the flavorful sauce.
In some regions, tamarind is added to curry for a subtle tangy note.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health and help reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish curry supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Turmeric, cumin, and coriander contain polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Ginger and garlic, common in the sauce, promote gastric juice production.

items.title: Fish or seafood allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to fish may experience severe reactions when consuming this dish.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared curry sauces can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Spice heat
items.content: Strong spices may irritate the stomach of those with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly stored fish can harbor bacteria and toxins.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the fish curry hot, ladling the sauce over a bed of rice. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, and a sprinkle of toasted cashews for crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of water or coconut milk to restore the creamy consistency.

content.title: About
content.content: Fish sticks are a ready‑to‑eat product made from white fish fillet that is minced, breaded, and partially fried. They are a convenient way to add fish to the diet, especially for children.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first fish sticks were introduced in the United States in the 1950s as a way to use fish trimmings.
Common fish used include cod, pollock, or hake, along with starch and seasonings.
The coating often contains wheat flour, but gluten‑free versions are available.
Fish sticks can be stored frozen for up to 12 months.
In some countries they are called “fish‑strips” or “fish‑sticks.”

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Fish sticks provide high‑quality animal protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Depending on the fish species, they may contain beneficial omega‑3s that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish is rich in B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They supply phosphorus, selenium, and iodine, important for bones, thyroid function, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: For those monitoring carb intake, fish sticks are relatively low in carbohydrates.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish or seafood.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The breading and additives often contain salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Trans fats and additives
items.content: Certain brands use partially hydrogenated oils, which may contain trans fats.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Preservatives and flavor enhancers may be present and not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fish sticks are typically baked or pan‑fried until golden brown. Serve them with mashed potatoes, a vegetable salad, tartar sauce, or simple ketchup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen fish sticks in an airtight bag at –18 °C. After thawing, consume within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Lime juice 100 % is a natural juice extracted from ripe limes, pasteurized and packaged in cans or glass bottles. The juice retains the fruit’s bright aroma, tanginess, and vitamin profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lime belongs to the citrus family and grows in tropical and subtropical regions.
Lime juice is a staple in Asian, Latin American, and Caribbean cuisines.
Pasteurization extends shelf life up to 12 months without added preservatives.
It is a key ingredient in classic cocktails such as Margarita and Mojito.
Compared with lemon juice, lime juice has a slightly sweeter, more vibrant acidity.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One hundred milliliters of lime juice provides about 30 mg of vitamin C, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and limonene in the juice help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity stimulates gastric juice production, improving food digestion.

items.title: May reduce kidney stone risk
items.content: Citric acid can help dissolve small calcium crystals, lowering stone formation.

items.title: Supports weight management
items.content: Low‑calorie beverage that can replace higher‑calorie sauces and marinades.

items.title: Acid reflux
items.content: People with high stomach acidity may experience increased heartburn after consuming lime juice.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may have an allergic reaction to lime.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Acidity can affect absorption of certain drugs, such as some antibiotics.

items.title: Added sugar in some products
items.content: Commercial versions may contain added sugars; check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use lime juice in marinades, sauces, salad dressings, cocktails, and desserts. Add it to water for a refreshing drink or as a flavor boost in baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans or bottles in a cool, dark place. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5–7 days.

pizza-with-meat-and-vegetables-from-rest.title: Pizza with meat and vegetables, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: Thin‑crust pizza with meat and vegetables is a fast‑food dish made from a crisp, thin dough topped with tomato sauce, slices of ham, sausage, chicken breast, and fresh vegetables such as bell pepper, onion, mushrooms and olives. The pizza is baked at high temperature, giving it a golden crust and juicy toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust cooks quickly, usually in 5–7 minutes in a professional oven.
The combination of meat and vegetables provides a balanced flavor and nutrition profile.
In Italy a similar style is called "pizza romana," known for its crunchy base.
Tomato sauce and mozzarella cheese supply lycopene and calcium.
Meat‑and‑vegetable pizza is often offered in fast‑food chains as a “complete” option with protein, veggies, and carbs.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meats such as ham, sausage and chicken provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, while cheese contributes calcium and phosphorus.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from the crust quickly replenish glycogen stores, useful for active lifestyles.

items.title: Lower fat in the crust
items.content: A thin crust contains less fat than a traditional thick crust, reducing overall calorie count.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant with potential health benefits.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed meats like sausage and ham are often high in salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some meats and cheese can increase saturated fat intake, which should be monitored in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Mozzarella may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The dough contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices. Fresh basil or oregano can be added for extra aroma. Optionally sprinkle grated Parmesan or drizzle with olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.
